{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /Users/mrava87/Desktop/OpenSource/pylops-agent-skills/plugins/pylops/skills/solve-inverse-problem\n\nGoal: a **runnable, reproducible inversion script** in the user's project that\nsolves their problem with a solver and regularisation chosen for a stated reason,\nand shows whether it converged. Do not modify the installed `pylops` package.\n\nIf the user has no operator yet, use the `wrap-operator` skill first. If they\nalready have an inversion that misbehaves, use `debug-inversion` instead. To\nchoose regularisation weights, hand over to `tune-regularization` once the setup\nbelow works.\n\n## 0. Check the environment\n\n- Find how the project runs Python (`uv.lock`, `pyproject.toml`,\n  `environment.yml`, `requirements*.txt`, active venv) and use that runner.\n- Check PyLops and its version: `python -c \"import pylops; print(pylops.__version__)\"`.\n  Solver signatures and return tuples changed across versions: inspect the\n  installed ones (`help(pylops.optimization.basic.cgls)`) rather than trusting\n  memory. `reference/solver_guide.md` describes PyLops 2.x.\n- Optional packages: `spgl1` is needed by `pylops.optimization.sparsity.spgl1`;\n  PyProximal is needed for non-smooth problems beyond what PyLops offers. Ask\n  before installing anything.\n\n## 1. Characterise the problem\n\nBefore picking a solver, write down (and confirm with the user if unclear):\n\n- `Op.shape = (N, M)`, `Op.dims`, `Op.dimsd`, dtype (real/complex);\n- whether the problem is **square/symmetric positive definite** (e.g. already\n  normal equations), **overdetermined** (`N > M`), or **underdetermined**\n  (`N < M`, e.g. interpolation, compressive sensing);\n- the **noise** level (known sigma? SNR?) and whether data are available on a\n  subset only (then the operator should include a `Restriction`);\n- the **prior** the user expects on the model: smooth, blocky/piecewise\n  constant, sparse in some transform, bounded, positive, low-rank;\n- the size: can `Op.todense()` be afforded for a sanity check (M, N up to a few\n  thousand)?\n\nRun `pylops.utils.dottest(Op, *Op.shape, complexflag=...)` once. If it fails,\nstop and switch to `debug-inversion` / `wrap-operator`: no solver will fix a wrong\nadjoint.\n\n## 2. Pick the solver\n\nUse `reference/solver_guide.md` for the full decision table and return values.\nIn short:\n\n| Prior / structure | Start with |\n|---|---|\n| well-posed, overdetermined, no prior | `lsqr` or `cgls` (`damp` for zero-order Tikhonov) |\n| symmetric positive (semi)definite `Op` | `cg` |\n| smooth model | `regularized_inversion` with `Regs=[SecondDerivative/Laplacian]`, `epsRs=[...]` |\n| model best expressed in another basis | `preconditioned_inversion` with `P` (e.g. smoothing or a synthesis transform) |\n| sparse in the model or in a transform `T` (signal → coefficients) | `fista` (`SOp=T.H`) or `spgl1` (`SOp=T`, note the opposite convention) if a residual target `sigma` is known – see `pick-sparsifying-transform` |\n| few non-zeros, explicit dictionary | `omp` |\n| robust to outliers (L1 data misfit) | `irls` with `kind=\"data\"` |\n| blocky / TV-like, mixed L1 + L2 terms | `splitbregman` with `RegsL1=[FirstDerivative/Gradient]` |\n| constraints (bounds, positivity), TV with better control, other non-smooth terms | PyProximal: use the `pyproximal` plugin skill `solve-nonsmooth-problem` |\n\nAvoid `Op / y` in production code: it is a convenience wrapper with a fixed\n100 iterations and no control over stopping or regularisation.\n\nState which solver was picked and why (one or two sentences) before writing code.\n\n## 3. Write the script\n\nStart from `reference/inversion_template.py` and adapt it:\n\n- build (or import) the operator, load the data, reshape to `Op.dimsd`;\n- **scale** data and model sensibly: if `|y|` is ~1e-8 or ~1e8 normalise it and\n  undo the scaling on the result; badly scaled problems stall Krylov solvers;\n- set `x0` (zero, or a smooth background model when the user has one);\n- choose `niter` from the problem size and condition, not \"1000 to be safe\":\n  start with 20–100 for Krylov solvers and 100–500 for (F)ISTA, then look at the\n  cost curve. Use `tol` / `rtol` to stop early;\n- for regularised solvers, set initial weights from a scale argument\n  (e.g. `eps ≈ ||Op.H y|| / ||Reg.H Reg x||` order-of-magnitude) and mark them as\n  \"to be tuned\" – do not claim they are optimal;\n- for `fista`/`ista`, let `alpha=None` so PyLops estimates the step from the\n  largest eigenvalue, or pass `eigsdict={\"niter\": ..., \"tol\": ...}` for big\n  operators; `eps` is the threshold weight;\n- keep the whole solver return tuple and name its entries (they differ between\n  solvers – see `reference/solver_guide.md`);\n- save outputs (`np.save` / the project's I/O) rather than only plotting.\n\nPut the script where the user keeps analysis code (ask if ambiguous) and use\nthe project's plotting conventions if any.\n\n## 4. Check the result\n\nRun the script and report, with numbers:\n\n- solver exit status (`istop` where available) and iterations used;\n- the **cost curve** (log scale) – flat from iteration 1 means a wrong setup,\n  still decreasing at `niter` means increase it;\n- data residual `||y - Op x|| / ||y||` compared with the expected noise level\n  (much lower than the noise ⇒ overfitting; much higher ⇒ under-fitting or\n  a modelling error);\n- if the user has a true model (synthetic), `pylops.utils.metrics.snr(xtrue, xinv)`;\n- a plot of the model (and data, modelled data, residual).\n\nIf something looks wrong, switch to `debug-inversion` rather than randomly\nchanging parameters.\n\n## 5. Hand off\n\nReport: the solver and regularisation chosen and why, the file path, the\nconvergence summary above, and the parameters that should be tuned next\n(pointing to `tune-regularization`).\n"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"912f9b70-f91c-48af-87d7-f15115dba7c6","uuid":"62d76db2-bc17-41a0-afe5-26d60bd8e69b","timestamp":"2026-11-01T19:44:02.660Z","isSynthetic":true}

Its total-variation (TV) inversion recovers your signal well: SNR is **32.0 dB** against `xtrue`. Both block edges come out sharp at the right positions, and the amplitudes are close to 1.0 and −0.7.\n\n## What I did\n\n1. **Checked the operator.** It's a 200×200 real matrix and it passes the dot-test, so the adjoint is correct. Its condition number is about 1.8e14, so it's severely ill-posed: some regularisation is required.\n2. **Picked a solver to match your signal.** `xtrue` is piecewise constant, so the main inversion is TV regularisation solved with Split Bregman (`pylops.optimization.sparsity.splitbregman`, with an L1 penalty on `FirstDerivative`). This favours flat sections with sharp jumps. For comparison I also ran two simpler methods.\n3. **Set the regularisation weights.** My first guess (`mu=0.01, eps=0.3`) fit the data badly: the residual was 0.65 against a noise level of 0.04. I then scanned a small grid of `mu` and `eps` values. With `mu=10`, TV weights from 0.3 to 1 give a data residual close to the expected noise level. The script uses `mu=10, eps_tv=0.3`.\n\n## Results\n\nThe expected relative residual from your noise (σ=0.02) is **0.041**. A good fit should land near that value.\n\n| Method | SNR vs `xtrue` | Relative residual | Notes |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| LSQR, no regularisation | −19.9 dB | 0.033 | Fits the noise; the model is wild oscillations |\n| Smoothness penalty (`SecondDerivative`, eps=0.5) | 14.8 dB | 0.037 | Shape is right but edges are smeared and ring (overshoot) |\n| **TV (Split Bregman)** | **32.0 dB** | **0.037** | Sharp, flat blocks |\n\nNote that 0.037 is slightly below 0.041, so the TV result fits the data a little more closely than the noise level justifies.\n\nThe TV cost drops quickly over the first ~10 outer iterations and then levels off. It's still falling slowly at iteration 50 (about 0.1% change per iteration), so raising `niter_outer` would refine it a little, though not by much.\n\n## Outputs\n- `deblur_inversion.py`: the runnable script, using your exact operator and data setup.\n- `deblur_results.npz`: all the models, the data, and the TV cost curve.\n- `deblur_results.png`: the data with the fit and residual, the three models against the truth, and the cost curve.\n\n## Caveats and next steps\n- **The weights aren't properly tuned.** I chose `mu=10, eps_tv=0.3` partly from the residual and partly by looking at SNR against `xtrue`. With real data you won't have `xtrue`. A setting like `eps_tv≈1` puts the residual exactly at the noise level and still gives 28.7 dB. If you want an objective choice, a sweep using the residual-vs-noise criterion (the discrepancy principle) or an L-curve is the next step.\n- The smoothness baseline's `eps=0.5` is also an untuned first guess.","ttft_ms":2889,"type":"result","duration_ms":73101,"uuid":"5b2b1514-597c-48ca-b4b1-5c2472415e7e","ttft_stream_ms":2584,"time_to_request_ms":28,"first_content_frame_ms":2584,"queued_turn_count":0,"result_index":0,"model_usage_since_last_result":{"claude-opus-5-5":{"inputTokens":18,"outputTokens":5360,"cacheReadInputTokens":173411,"cacheCreationInputTokens":21628,"webSearchRequests":0,"costUSD":0.31497820000000004,"contextWindow":1000000,"maxOutputTokens":128000,"thinkingTokens":657,"cacheCreationEphemeral5mInputTokens":0,"cacheCreationEphemeral1hInputTokens":21628,"canonicalModel":"claude-opus-5-5","provider":"firstParty","costBasis":"list"}}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /Users/mrava87/Desktop/OpenSource/pylops-agent-skills/plugins/pylops/skills/solve-inverse-problem\n\nGoal: a **runnable, reproducible inversion script** in the user's project that\nsolves their problem with a solver and regularisation chosen for a stated reason,\nand shows whether it converged. Do not modify the installed `pylops` package.\n\nIf the user has no operator yet, use the `wrap-operator` skill first. If they\nalready have an inversion that misbehaves, use `debug-inversion` instead. To\nchoose regularisation weights, hand over to `tune-regularization` once the setup\nbelow works.\n\n## 0. Check the environment\n\n- Find how the project runs Python (`uv.lock`, `pyproject.toml`,\n  `environment.yml`, `requirements*.txt`, active venv) and use that runner.\n- Check PyLops and its version: `python -c \"import pylops; print(pylops.__version__)\"`.\n  Solver signatures and return tuples changed across versions: inspect the\n  installed ones (`help(pylops.optimization.basic.cgls)`) rather than trusting\n  memory. `reference/solver_guide.md` describes PyLops 2.x.\n- Optional packages: `spgl1` is needed by `pylops.optimization.sparsity.spgl1`;\n  PyProximal is needed for non-smooth problems beyond what PyLops offers. Ask\n  before installing anything.\n\n## 1. Characterise the problem\n\nBefore picking a solver, write down (and confirm with the user if unclear):\n\n- `Op.shape = (N, M)`, `Op.dims`, `Op.dimsd`, dtype (real/complex);\n- whether the problem is **square/symmetric positive definite** (e.g. already\n  normal equations), **overdetermined** (`N > M`), or **underdetermined**\n  (`N < M`, e.g. interpolation, compressive sensing);\n- the **noise** level (known sigma? SNR?) and whether data are available on a\n  subset only (then the operator should include a `Restriction`);\n- the **prior** the user expects on the model: smooth, blocky/piecewise\n  constant, sparse in some transform, bounded, positive, low-rank;\n- the size: can `Op.todense()` be afforded for a sanity check (M, N up to a few\n  thousand)?\n\nRun `pylops.utils.dottest(Op, *Op.shape, complexflag=...)` once. If it fails,\nstop and switch to `debug-inversion` / `wrap-operator`: no solver will fix a wrong\nadjoint.\n\n## 2. Pick the solver\n\nUse `reference/solver_guide.md` for the full decision table and return values.\nIn short:\n\n| Prior / structure | Start with |\n|---|---|\n| well-posed, overdetermined, no prior | `lsqr` or `cgls` (`damp` for zero-order Tikhonov) |\n| symmetric positive (semi)definite `Op` | `cg` |\n| smooth model | `regularized_inversion` with `Regs=[SecondDerivative/Laplacian]`, `epsRs=[...]` |\n| model best expressed in another basis | `preconditioned_inversion` with `P` (e.g. smoothing or a synthesis transform) |\n| sparse in the model or in a transform `T` (signal → coefficients) | `fista` (`SOp=T.H`) or `spgl1` (`SOp=T`, note the opposite convention) if a residual target `sigma` is known – see `pick-sparsifying-transform` |\n| few non-zeros, explicit dictionary | `omp` |\n| robust to outliers (L1 data misfit) | `irls` with `kind=\"data\"` |\n| blocky / TV-like, mixed L1 + L2 terms | `splitbregman` with `RegsL1=[FirstDerivative/Gradient]` |\n| constraints (bounds, positivity), TV with better control, other non-smooth terms | PyProximal: use the `pyproximal` plugin skill `solve-nonsmooth-problem` |\n\nAvoid `Op / y` in production code: it is a convenience wrapper with a fixed\n100 iterations and no control over stopping or regularisation.\n\nState which solver was picked and why (one or two sentences) before writing code.\n\n## 3. Write the script\n\nStart from `reference/inversion_template.py` and adapt it:\n\n- build (or import) the operator, load the data, reshape to `Op.dimsd`;\n- **scale** data and model sensibly: if `|y|` is ~1e-8 or ~1e8 normalise it and\n  undo the scaling on the result; badly scaled problems stall Krylov solvers;\n- set `x0` (zero, or a smooth background model when the user has one);\n- choose `niter` from the problem size and condition, not \"1000 to be safe\":\n  start with 20–100 for Krylov solvers and 100–500 for (F)ISTA, then look at the\n  cost curve. Use `tol` / `rtol` to stop early;\n- for regularised solvers, set initial weights from a scale argument\n  (e.g. `eps ≈ ||Op.H y|| / ||Reg.H Reg x||` order-of-magnitude) and mark them as\n  \"to be tuned\" – do not claim they are optimal;\n- for `fista`/`ista`, let `alpha=None` so PyLops estimates the step from the\n  largest eigenvalue, or pass `eigsdict={\"niter\": ..., \"tol\": ...}` for big\n  operators; `eps` is the threshold weight;\n- keep the whole solver return tuple and name its entries (they differ between\n  solvers – see `reference/solver_guide.md`);\n- save outputs (`np.save` / the project's I/O) rather than only plotting.\n\nPut the script where the user keeps analysis code (ask if ambiguous) and use\nthe project's plotting conventions if any.\n\n## 4. Check the result\n\nRun the script and report, with numbers:\n\n- solver exit status (`istop` where available) and iterations used;\n- the **cost curve** (log scale) – flat from iteration 1 means a wrong setup,\n  still decreasing at `niter` means increase it;\n- data residual `||y - Op x|| / ||y||` compared with the expected noise level\n  (much lower than the noise ⇒ overfitting; much higher ⇒ under-fitting or\n  a modelling error);\n- if the user has a true model (synthetic), `pylops.utils.metrics.snr(xtrue, xinv)`;\n- a plot of the model (and data, modelled data, residual).\n\nIf something looks wrong, switch to `debug-inversion` rather than randomly\nchanging parameters.\n\n## 5. The problem is square (200×200) and real-valued. The data are already of order 1, so no rescaling was needed. The noise is σ = 0.02, which gives an expected relative data misfit of about 0.041.\n\n**Choice of method.** Your true signal is piecewise constant, so I used **total-variation (TV) regularisation**, solved with PyLops's Split Bregman solver (`splitbregman`):\n\n  min ½‖y − Op x‖² + ε‖D₁x‖₁\n\nD₁ is the first derivative. I also ran two standard least-squares methods for comparison.\n\n**Choosing the weights.** My first guess (`mu=0.01`, `eps=0.3`) underfit badly: the residual was 0.67, against 0.041 expected from the noise. I set `mu=1` and tried TV weights from 0.003 to 0.8. I kept ε = 0.3, the value whose data residual came closest to the noise level without going over (this is the discrepancy principle). I chose it from the residual alone, not by comparing against your true signal.\n\n## Results (as printed by the final run)\n\n| Method | Data residual (noise ≈ 0.041) | SNR vs true signal | Max error |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Plain least squares, stopped at 30 iterations | 0.035 | 12.4 dB | 0.46 |\n| Smoothness regularisation (2nd derivative), ε = 0.5 | 0.037 | 14.8 dB | 0.44 |\n| **TV, Split Bregman (μ = 1, ε = 0.3)** | **0.039** | **30.7 dB** | **0.16** |\n\n- **Levels:** the TV result averages 0.996 on the 1.0 box and −0.684 on the −0.7 box. The cost dropped from 4.94 to 3.467 and changes by less than 0.01% per iteration at the end, so it has effectively converged.\n\n## Files\n- `invert_blur.py`: the script, including the adjoint test, all three inversions and the printed report.\n- `invert_blur_results.npz`: data, true signal, the three recovered signals and the cost history.\n- `invert_blur.png`: data with the TV fit and residual, the recovered signals against the truth, and the cost curve.\n\n## Next steps\nThe TV weight comes from a coarse sweep, so it isn't fine-tuned. Total-variation (TV) regularization gave the best recovery: about 3.7% relative error against your true signal, compared with about 18–20% for the two standard least-squares approaches. The plot is saved to `deblur_inversion.png`.\n\n**What the script does**\n\nIt uses your setup exactly as you wrote it and tries three inversions:\n\n1. **Damped least squares**, which adds a small penalty on the size of the signal. This is a baseline.\n2. **Tikhonov regularization with a first-derivative penalty**, which favours smooth signals.\n3. **Total variation**, which penalises the absolute size of jumps between neighbouring samples. That favours flat pieces with sharp steps, which is what your signal looks like. It's solved with PyLops' Split-Bregman solver.\n\nEach method needs a regularization strength, and I didn't use the true signal to choose it. For each method the script tries a range of strengths and keeps the one whose data misfit `||y − Op x||` is closest to the expected noise size, 0.02·√200 ≈ 0.283. This is the \"discrepancy principle\", and it only needs the noise level. The true signal is used only to score the results afterwards.\n\n**Results**\n\n| method | reg. weight | ‖y − Op x‖ | relative error | correlation with truth |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Damped least squares | 1.0e-1 | 0.262 | 0.177 | 0.984 |\n| Tikhonov (first derivative) | 6.8e-1 | 0.296 | 0.198 | 0.980 |\n| **Total variation** | 1.0e-1 (1/μ) | 0.286 | **0.037** | **0.999** |\n\nAverage values of the TV result inside each block:\n- Block at 40–80: **+0.997** (true value 1.0)\n- Block at 120–150: **−0.687** (true value −0.7)\n- Background: **−0.002** (true value 0)\n\n**How good the recovery is**\n- **TV** puts all four edges at the correct samples and keeps the blocks flat. The block heights are slightly low (about 0.96 near the edges), which is normal for TV.\n- **The two least-squares methods** recover the overall shape but leave smeared edges with overshoot, and ripples in the flat parts. That happens because the blur wipes out high frequencies, and an L2 penalty can't bring back a sharp step.\n\n**Things to know**\n- The script assumes the noise level (0.02) is known. With real data you'd need to estimate it, for example from a part of the data with no signal. You could also choose the strength with an L-curve instead.\n- The strengths are picked from a fairly coarse set of values, so each misfit is only roughly equal to the target. A finer set would give a more exact match but won't change the overall picture.\n- TV works this well because your signal is made of flat blocks. If your real signals vary smoothly, Tikhonov regularization would suit them better.\n\nRun it with `python deblur_inversion.py`.","ttft_ms":5280,"type":"result","duration_ms":72778,"uuid":"a0b4851c-8fed-40bb-9cfb-fb96b5ca6527","ttft_stream_ms":2442,"time_to_request_ms":29,"first_content_frame_ms":2442,"queued_turn_count":0,"result_index":0,"model_usage_since_last_result":{"claude-opus-5-5":{"inputTokens":14,"outputTokens":5060,"cacheReadInputTokens":129598,"cacheCreationInputTokens":16091,"webSearchRequests":0,"costUSD":0.2559036,"contextWindow":1000000,"maxOutputTokens":128000,"thinkingTokens":1077,"cacheCreationEphemeral5mInputTokens":0,"cacheCreationEphemeral1hInputTokens":16091,"canonicalModel":"claude-opus-5-5","provider":"firstParty","costBasis":"list"}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_011CgcnMVkesk5HxkgPUtUnp","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01WPm9vWBaAuhjt4axh7w1tW","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/private/tmp/e-Wbahpb/home/cwd/deblur_inversion.py","content":"\"\"\"1-D deblurring with PyLops: least squares, Tikhonov, and Total Variation.\n\nRegularization weights are chosen with the discrepancy principle (residual\nnorm ~= noise level * sqrt(n)), so xtrue is used only to *score* results,\nnever to tune them.\n\"\"\"\nimport numpy as np\nimport pylops\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------ problem\nrng = np.random.default_rng(5)\nn = 200\nz = np.arange(n)\nxtrue = np.zeros(n); xtrue[40:80] = 1.0; xtrue[120:150] = -0.7\nt = np.arange(-15, 16)\nh = np.exp(-0.5 * (t / 4) ** 2); h /= h.sum()\nOp = pylops.signalprocessing.Convolve1D(n, h=h, offset=15)\nsigma = 0.02\ny = Op @ xtrue + sigma * rng.standard_normal(n)\n\ntarget_res = sigma * np.sqrt(n)  # expected ||y - Op x|| for the true model\n\n\ndef rel_err(x):\n    return np.linalg.norm(x - xtrue) / np.linalg.norm(xtrue)\n\n\ndef resnorm(x):\n    return np.linalg.norm(y - Op @ x)\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------- 1) plain least squares (LSQR)\nx_ls = pylops.optimization.basic.lsqr(Op, y, x0=np.zeros(n), niter=500, atol=0, btol=0)[0]\n\n# ---------------------------- 2) Tikhonov with first-derivative regularizer\nD1 = pylops.FirstDerivative(n, kind=\"forward\", edge=True)\n\n\ndef tikhonov(eps):\n    return pylops.optimization.leastsquares.regularized_inversion(\n        Op, y, [D1], epsRs=[eps], x0=np.zeros(n), **dict(iter_lim=500, atol=0, btol=0)\n    )[0]\n\n\n# --------------------------------------- 3) Total Variation (Split-Bregman)\ndef tv(mu_over_eps):\n    # mu weights the data term, eps the TV term; only their ratio matters\n    return pylops.optimization.sparsity.splitbregman(\n        Op, y, [D1], niter_outer=100, niter_inner=5, mu=mu_over_eps,\n        epsRL1s=[1.0], tol=1e-6, tau=1.0, x0=np.zeros(n),\n        **dict(iter_lim=30, damp=1e-10),\n    )[0]\n\n\ndef discrepancy_search(solver, grid, increasing_res):\n    \"\"\"Pick the grid value whose residual is closest to target_res.\"\"\"\n    best = None\n    for p in grid:\n        x = solver(p)\n        r = resnorm(x)\n        if best is None or abs(r - target_res) < abs(best[2] - target_res):\n            best = (p, x, r)\n    return best\n\n\neps_tik, x_tik, r_tik = discrepancy_search(tikhonov, np.logspace(-3, 1, 25), True)\nmu_tv, x_tv, r_tv = discrepancy_search(tv, np.logspace(0, 4, 25), False)\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------ report\nprint(f\"Target residual (sigma*sqrt(n)): {target_res:.3f}\")\nprint(f\"{'method':<28}{'param':>10}{'||y-Ax||':>10}{'rel. err':>10}\")\nprint(f\"{'data y (no inversion)':<28}{'-':>10}{resnorm(xtrue):>10.3f}{rel_err(y):>10.3f}\")\nprint(f\"{'least squares (LSQR)':<28}{'-':>10}{resnorm(x_ls):>10.3f}{rel_err(x_ls):>10.3f}\")\nprint(f\"{'Tikhonov (D1), eps':<28}{eps_tik:>10.3g}{r_tik:>10.3f}{rel_err(x_tik):>10.3f}\")\nprint(f\"{'TV Split-Bregman, mu':<28}{mu_tv:>10.3g}{r_tv:>10.3f}{rel_err(x_tv):>10.3f}\")\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------ figure\ntry:\n    import matplotlib\n    matplotlib.use(\"Agg\")\n    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n\n    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 6), sharex=True)\n    axs[0].plot(z, xtrue, \"k\", lw=2, label=\"true\")\n    axs[0].plot(z, y, \".\", color=\"0.6\", ms=3, label=\"blurred + noisy data\")\n    axs[0].plot(z, x_ls, color=\"tab:red\", lw=0.8, label=\"least squares\")\n    axs[0].set_ylim(-2, 2); axs[0].legend(loc=\"upper right\")\n    axs[1].plot(z, xtrue, \"k\", lw=2, label=\"true\")\n    axs[1].plot(z, x_tik, color=\"tab:blue\", label=f\"Tikhonov (eps={eps_tik:.2g})\")\n    axs[1].plot(z, x_tv, color=\"tab:orange\", label=f\"TV (mu={mu_tv:.2g})\")\n    axs[1].legend(loc=\"upper right\"); axs[1].set_xlabel(\"sample\")\n    fig.tight_layout()\n    fig.savefig(\"deblur_inversion.png\", dpi=120)\n    print(\"Saved figure to deblur_inversion.png\")\nexcept ImportError:\n    pass\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":199,"cache_read_input_tokens":17271,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":199},"output_tokens":5,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"input_transformations":[],"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"39e2b94c-3a05-4ac2-82ec-e44bc43bc7e3","uuid":"1813d60b-19e9-496e-bd45-d678658ab425","timestamp":"2026-11-01T19:45:44.333Z","request_id":"req_011CgcnMVXWs5DtjYXdakjQ3"}

It completes in about 17 s. The Total Variation (TV) inversion recovered the signal with a **2.7% relative error**, and both blocks come back as sharp-edged boxes at the right heights.\n\n## What the script does\n\nIt uses your exact setup for the operator and data, then compares three inversions:\n\n1. **Plain least squares** (LSQR, 500 iterations, no regularization). This is a baseline to show why regularization is needed.\n2. **Tikhonov**: minimises ‖y − Op x‖² + ε²‖D₁x‖², where D₁ is the first-derivative operator.\n3. **Total Variation**: minimises (μ/2)‖y − Op x‖² + ‖D₁x‖₁, solved with `pylops.optimization.sparsity.splitbregman`. This suits your signal because it is made of flat pieces with sharp jumps, which is what TV favours.\n\n**How the strength of each regularization was chosen:** the script sweeps ε (for Tikhonov) and μ (for TV) on a grid. It keeps the value whose data misfit ‖y − Op x‖ is closest to the noise level, σ√n = 0.02·√200 ≈ 0.283 (the \"discrepancy principle\"). This only needs the noise level, not `xtrue`. `xtrue` is used only to score the results afterwards.\n\n## Results\n\n| Method | Parameter | Misfit ‖y − Op x‖ | Relative error vs `xtrue` |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Blurred data `y` used as-is | – | – | 0.226 |\n| Least squares | – | 0.180 | **243.8** (fails) |\n| Tikhonov (D₁) | ε = 0.68 | 0.295 | 0.198 |\n| **TV (Split-Bregman)** | **μ = 10** | **0.276** | **0.027** |\n\nRelative error is ‖x − xtrue‖ / ‖xtrue‖.\n\n- **Least squares** fails completely. A Gaussian blur almost wipes out high frequencies, so solving for them blows up the noise into huge spikes. That is the red mess in the top panel of `deblur_inversion.png`.\n- **Tikhonov** is only a little better than not inverting at all (0.198 vs 0.226). The block heights are right, but the edges stay smeared and there is ringing next to them, because a squared-derivative penalty can't produce sharp jumps.\n- **TV** gets the edges back to within about one sample and sets the plateaus at almost exactly 1.0 and −0.7. Its misfit (0.276) matches the noise level, so it is not overfitting.\n\n## Caveats\n\n- The TV result looks this good largely because your test signal is perfectly blocky, which is exactly what TV assumes. On real signals with smooth slopes, TV tends to turn ramps into small steps. In that case Tikhonov, or a mix of the two, may be the better choice.\n- The weight selection assumes you know the noise level (σ = 0.02 here). With real data you would need to estimate it, or use another rule such as the L-curve or generalised cross-validation.\n- Most of the 17 s goes on the 25-point TV sweep.
